samples.question: This image shows one flight of steps drawn in side view on white paper as a single solid block of ONE STRONG COLOUR standing on a grey ground line. The flat top of each step is a TREAD; the treads are the level coloured edges along the top of the block, all of the same width, and there are between four and nine of them. Read the treads from the LEFT edge of the block to the RIGHT edge. One tread is HIGHER than another when its coloured top edge is drawn nearer the top edge of the page. Judge only the top edges of the coloured block: the thin grey rail above the flight always slopes upward to the right and is decoration, and so are the grey page frame, the grey corner ticks, the small grey diamonds and the small coloured square near the top right corner. Whether the flight climbs all the way is chosen separately from the number of treads, the tread width, the colour, the tallest step, the total amount of coloured ink and the position on the page, so on some pages the flight climbs the whole way and on other pages one tread is drawn lower than the tread just before it, and neither is a mistake. No image in this set is a borderline case: neighbouring treads are never drawn at the same height. Report the picture in front of you, and do not answer from how a flight of steps is usually built. Going from left to right, is every tread higher than the tread just before it? Answer yes or no.
